title: How To Avoid A Big, Ugly Bad Day
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a familiar warning sign: a class that hasn't technically broken any rules but shows a subtle shift in attitude — a little more carelessness, a little less energy — that experienced teachers sense intuitively, referencing Malcolm Gladwell's concept of a "blink" moment. He warns against the common response of stopping to lecture or warn, since technically no boundary has been crossed and students will feel it's unfair. His recommended fix is instead to back up to the most recent transition or routine and cheerfully re-teach it with the same enthusiasm used the first week of school, modeling it again and having students practice until it's done well. He frames well-taught routines as the mechanism that transfers excellence and alertness across the whole classroom, correcting the vague "off" feeling before it snowballs into a genuinely bad day.
points: A subtle shift in class mood or attitude — without any actual rule violation — is a warning sign worth acting on immediately.
Lecturing or warning at this stage is a mistake, since no rule has technically been broken and students will feel it's unfair.
The fix is to back up to the nearest transition or routine and cheerfully re-teach it with first-week-of-school enthusiasm.
Well-taught routines are described as the mechanism that transfers excellence and alertness across the whole classroom.
quotes: No rules are broken, but there is an attitude or mood in their demeanor you can’t quite put your finger on.
You know that if you leave it alone, if you allow your class to continue down the path they’re headed, then a bad day is just around the corner.
The author Malcolm Gladwell wrote a book about this gut feeling called Blink .
But the problem with this approach is that your boundary lines of behavior, as defined by your classroom management plan , were never actually crossed.
The solution is to back up to the previous transition and cheerfully teach that routine again.
Remember, well-taught routines transfer excellence to everything you do.
It fixes that off-kilter feeling you can’t quite put your finger on.
